patient.chief_complaint: Increasing difficulty with balance and slowness of movement over the past year
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sunita Reddy is a 64-year-old right-handed dental hygienist presenting to the neurology clinic with a one-year history of progressive gait unsteadiness and generalized slowness of movement. Her wife, who accompanies her, first noticed that she was walking more slowly approximately 12 to 14 months ago and seemed to be shuffling her feet at times, particularly in the morning. Over the past six months, she has become noticeably slower in her daily activities, taking longer to dress, button her shirts, and complete meals. Her wife reports that her handwriting has become slightly smaller, though she attributes this to arthritis in her hands. She has had two near-falls in the past three months, both occurring when turning quickly, though she has not fallen to the ground. She denies any frank tremor, but her wife has occasionally noticed a mild shaking of her hands when she holds the newspaper up to read. She endorses some difficulty with constipation that predates her current complaints by approximately two years, as well as reduced sense of smell that she became aware of about a year ago when she could not smell a gas leak that her wife detected. She has also noticed some difficulty initiating sleep and her wife reports that she has become more restless at night, occasionally kicking and flailing her arms during sleep, which began roughly 18 months ago. Her mood has been lower over the past year; she has less motivation to engage in hobbies such as woodworking and fishing that she previously enjoyed. She was started on metoclopramide approximately two years ago by her gastroenterologist for diabetic gastroparesis with nausea and early satiety, which has improved her gastrointestinal symptoms. She takes this medication regularly three times daily. She is referred today by her primary care physician for evaluation of her progressive motor symptoms.

output.proposed: Assessment of metoclopramide interactions with current medications
interactions: Metoclopramide + dopamine-active medications: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine D2 receptors, directly antagonizing any dopaminergic therapy for PD. If carbidopa-levodopa is initiated, metoclopramide will reduce its clinical efficacy.
Metoclopramide + metformin: No significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Both affect GI motility in different ways.
Metoclopramide + glipizide: Metoclopramide may accelerate gastric emptying and alter absorption of sulfonylureas; glucose levels should be monitored.
contraindications: Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patients with Parkinson disease or underlying dopaminergic deficit — it exacerbates parkinsonism via D2 receptor blockade.
Metoclopramide should be discontinued immediately in this patient regardless of the final diagnosis (PD vs DIP vs metoclopramide-unmasked PD).
warnings: Chronic metoclopramide use (>12 weeks) carries FDA black box warning for tardive dyskinesia. This patient has been on it for 2 years.
Discontinuation should be gradual with gastroparesis monitoring; alternative prokinetics (domperidone where available, or low-dose erythromycin) should be discussed with gastroenterology.
Resolution of drug-induced parkinsonism after metoclopramide discontinuation may take weeks to months; if symptoms persist >6 months after discontinuation, underlying PD is more likely.
output.formulary_status: On formulary but FDA black box warning for chronic use; specialist review recommended
alternatives: Domperidone (available outside US) — peripheral D2 blocker with minimal CNS penetration; does not cause parkinsonism
Low-dose erythromycin (off-label) for gastroparesis; no dopaminergic effects
Dietary modifications: small, frequent, low-fat, low-fiber meals to aid gastric emptying

results.title: Differentiating Drug-Induced Parkinsonism from Parkinson Disease
results.key_finding: DIP is typically symmetric, develops within days to weeks of drug exposure, lacks non-motor prodromal features, and resolves within weeks to months after offending agent discontinuation

results.title: DaTscan Utility in Differentiating Neurodegenerative from Non-Neurodegenerative Parkinsonism
results.authors: Bajaj N, Hauser RA, Grachev ID
results.key_finding: DaTscan (Ioflupane I-123 SPECT) reliably distinguishes neurodegenerative parkinsonism (abnormal scan) from drug-induced parkinsonism (normal scan) with sensitivity 78-97% and specificity 80-100%

results.title: Prodromal Markers of Parkinson Disease
results.key_finding: REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, constipation, and depression may precede motor symptoms by years. Presence of multiple prodromal markers strongly supports underlying synucleinopathy rather than drug-induced parkinsonism

output.summary: The literature supports a systematic approach to differentiating PD from DIP: (1) assess symmetry of findings — PD is typically asymmetric, DIP symmetric; (2) evaluate prodromal non-motor features — presence of RBD, hyposmia, and constipation favors PD; (3) DaTscan is the most useful ancillary test, with abnormal results confirming presynaptic dopaminergic deficit and effectively ruling out pure DIP; (4) discontinuation of the offending agent with clinical monitoring over 6 months is recommended regardless.

sequence_constraints.reason: Identify the offending DA antagonist (metoclopramide) before relying on levodopa response to clarify diagnosis
Exclude vascular/NPH/structural mimics on MRI before committing to DaTscan-based PD confirmation

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, supportive features, no absolute exclusion criteria)
Document temporal sequence of motor and non-motor (REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic intolerance) features
Review the full medication list for dopamine receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antipsychotics) and any other agents that can mimic or worsen parkinsonism
Identify metoclopramide as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist and discontinue it; substitute ondansetron, prucalopride, erythromycin, or (where available) domperidone
Recognize that premotor features (RBD, constipation, hyposmia) preceding metoclopramide use point to underlying idiopathic PD rather than pure DIP
Use DaTscan to differentiate underlying neurodegenerative PD (abnormal scan) from pure DIP (normal scan)
Do not start levodopa while the patient remains on metoclopramide because of pharmacological antagonism
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea in a patient with parkinsonism

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict pharmacotherapy of psychosis to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
Do not continue metoclopramide in a patient with parkinsonism
Do not start levodopa while metoclopramide remains in the regimen
key_reasoning_points: Symmetric onset in a patient on metoclopramide creates diagnostic overlap between idiopathic PD and pure drug-induced parkinsonism
Premotor non-motor features that predate metoclopramide initiation point to underlying synucleinopathy
DaTscan is the critical differentiator: abnormal scan supports underlying neurodegenerative PD
RBD on polysomnography is a strong synucleinopathy biomarker and not caused by metoclopramide
Mother / family history of essential tremor (if present) is a red herring — ET and PD are distinct diseases
Metoclopramide has an FDA black-box warning against use beyond 12 weeks because of tardive dyskinesia risk

red_herrings.data_point: Active metoclopramide use for gastroparesis predating most motor symptoms
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor toward pure drug-induced parkinsonism and away from a neurodegenerative diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Premotor features (RBD, constipation, hyposmia) preceding metoclopramide and an abnormal DaTscan establish underlying PD; metoclopramide unmasks rather than causes the syndrome
ET and PD are distinct conditions; PD diagnosis is established by motor and supportive criteria irrespective of family ET
